stories.title: Stewards Sets Up $240M Deal for Two South Florida Multifamily Properties
stories.excerpt: Fort Lauderdale-based Stewards has signed letters of intent to acquire two apartment properties in Broward County, Fla., in a stock transaction valued at $240 million. The Nasdaq-listed financial and real estate company will acquire the 330-unit Pixl apartments in Plantation, and the 214-unit Envy apartments in Pompano Beach. Under the proposed structure, Stewards would acquire the equity interests in the entities that own the properties, and issue the sellers new stock at $3 per share. According to Stewards, the $240 million figure represents the properties’ aggregate implied value, including existing property-level debt, rather than the value of stock Stewards will issue for the deal. “This is an important next step in the execution of our broader Stewards strategy,” CEO and President Shaun Quin said in a statement, adding that the two properties would expand the company’s real assets platform as it builds across private credit, real estate and technology. Invesca Development Group developed both projects. Pixl at 4300 Northwest Ninth Court was completed in 2025, while Envy opened at 425 East Atlantic Boulevard in 2021. “Real assets have become an increasingly important part of what we are building at Stewards,” Chairman Glen Steward said. The deal comes days after Stewards uplisted to the Nasdaq Capital Market, where its shares began trading on Sept. 10. In 2025, when the firm operated as Favo Capital, it acquired the 1818 Park mixed-use building in Hollywood, Fla., in an all-stock deal valued at $190 million. Stewards refinanced that property in June with a $69 million senior mortgage and a $10 million mezzanine loan. Gregory Cornfield can be reached at gcornfield@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Stewards acquires 544 units (Pixl, Envy) in Broward County for ~$240M equity value
Fort Lauderdale firm issues stock at $3/share; both properties developed by Invesca
Deal expands Stewards' real assets platform across private credit, RE, and tech
stories.summary: Fort Lauderdale-based Stewards signed letters of intent to acquire two Broward County apartment properties—the 330-unit Pixl in Plantation and 214-unit Envy in Pompano Beach—in a stock transaction valued at $240 million (including existing debt). Stewards will issue sellers new stock at $3 per share. Both properties were developed by Invesca Development Group. The deal advances Stewards' strategy of building a broader real assets platform.
stories.impact: South Florida multifamily remains an acquisition target for publicly traded firms seeking near-institutional scale; however, Stewards' use of equity currency (stock issuance) rather than cash signals capital discipline amid potential rate/valuation uncertainty. Watch absorption and rent trajectory in Broward—tight supply and migration inflows support value-add thesis, but market saturation risk exists if development continues at pace.

Speakers include Joe Vargas, president, Wonderful Real Estate; Eugene Seroka, executive director, Port of Los Angeles; Rick Ellison, executive vice chairman, Cushman & Wakefield; and Brian Roach, director, asset and fund management, United States at Mapletree. bullets: Connect Industrial West 2026 panels covered advanced manufacturing, port investment, electricity costs

stories.summary: Connect Industrial West 2026 in Irvine featured industry leaders discussing advanced manufacturing growth in Southern California, the Port of Los Angeles' role in generating investment, electricity costs as a site-selection variable, and deal creativity. stories.impact: Electricity-cost sensitivity in site selection signals rising operational burden for tenant base (data centers, advanced manufacturing, logistics); may compress NOI and cap rates in high-power-cost submarkets. Industrial strength in SoCal's logistics corridor supports property values, but development ROI is tightening if power, land, and labor costs accelerate faster than rent. Multifamily in secondary inland markets (Inland Empire, San Bernardino) could benefit from industrial workforce draw-in.

stories.title: Related Launches Leasing for Tuxedo Luxury Rentals
stories.excerpt: Related Companies has officially begun its first phase of leasing for residences at The Village at Tuxedo Reserve, the mixed-use town center in the 1,200-acre Tuxedo Reserve community in New York’s Hudson Valley. Located 30 miles from Manhattan in Tuxedo, NY, the 336 luxury rental apartments will be integrated amid retail, dining, public gathering spaces, and year-round programming at The Village. “As we begin leasing our apartments at The Village at Tuxedo Reserve, we are one step closer to welcoming residents to this community,” said Greg Gushee, EVP at Related Companies. “We look forward to seeing this community flourish, serving residents, local businesses, and visitors for generations to come.” Anchored by Market Square, The Village will serve as a central gathering place for community events, seasonal programming, outdoor performances, farmers’ markets, and public celebrations throughout the year. The Village Green and seasonal skating rink will welcome local and surrounding community members year-round. The post Related Launches Leasing for Tuxedo Luxury Rentals appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Related Companies launches leasing for 336 luxury apartments at Tuxedo Reserve, Hudson Valley, NY
Mixed-use village site 30 miles from Manhattan includes retail, dining, public spaces; completion TBD
First phase leasing underway; project anchored by Market Square and community programming
stories.summary: Related Companies has begun leasing for the 336-unit luxury rental apartments at The Village at Tuxedo Reserve, a mixed-use town center on a 1,200-acre property in Tuxedo, NY, 30 miles north of Manhattan. The Village integrates residences with retail, dining, public gathering spaces, and year-round programming, anchored by Market Square. No delivery date specified.
stories.impact: Hudson Valley exurban multifamily targeting affluent renters (and potential reverse-commuters) signals developer confidence in remote-work permanence and suburban flight. Competition from masterplanned luxury communities in outlying metros may suppress rent growth and NOI in inner-ring suburbs; however, demographic aging and lifestyle preference shifts could sustain demand. Monitor lease velocity and concessions to gauge market absorption—slow leasing may indicate pricing ahead of actual demand or limited tenant pool within commute radius.

stories.title: Avatar Bridge Loan Finances Acquisition of Historic Providence Hotel
stories.excerpt: Avatar Financial Group LLC has provided a $6.45-million bridge loan to finance the acquisition of Hotel Providence, an 80-room boutique hotel in Downtown Providence, RI. The two-year, first-lien loan was originated at 63% loan-to-value. The hotel has operated without a brand affiliation since its Wyndham flag was discontinued in early 2025, and the prior owner did not complete a planned repositioning of the property. The resulting decline in occupancy created the opening for the sponsor, an experienced hotel owner and operator with an established presence in the Providence market, to acquire the hotel and improve it in stages. “This sponsor isn’t going to get another shot at a Downtown Providence hotel at this basis,” said T.R. Hazelrigg IV, Avatar’s president and co-founder. “The flag came off, occupancy went with it, and the last owner walked away from the repositioning. That’s what put the building within reach of an operator who actually works this market. Now he gets to choose a brand on his own schedule instead of somebody else’s.” Located at 139 Mathewson Street, the historic property dates to 1882, when it debuted as the Westminster Hotel. It sits in Providence’s Entertainment District. The post Avatar Bridge Loan Finances Acquisition of Historic Providence Hotel appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Avatar Financial provides $6.45M bridge loan for Hotel Providence acquisition at 63% LTV
80-room historic boutique hotel; prior Wyndham flag dropped early 2025, occupancy fell
Two-year first-lien loan; sponsor is experienced local operator repositioning without brand mandate
stories.summary: Avatar Financial provided a $6.45 million, two-year bridge loan at 63% LTV to finance acquisition of Hotel Providence, an 80-room boutique hotel in downtown Providence's Entertainment District. The property lost its Wyndham flag in early 2025, causing occupancy to decline; the prior owner abandoned a repositioning plan. The new sponsor is an established local hotel operator with flexibility to select a new brand.
stories.impact: Limited relevance to multifamily development. Hospitality distress (flag loss, owner exit) creates opportunity for experienced operators but does not directly signal apartment demand or supply shifts. However, Entertainment District revival in Providence could eventually drive mixed-use residential development—watch for ancillary multifamily projects if the hotel repositioning succeeds and anchors broader downtown revitalization.

stories.title: Local College Snaps Up Former Rite Aid in Barstow
stories.excerpt: Progressive Real Estate Partners represented a Southern California real estate developer in the sale of a 17,272-square-foot freestanding retail building located at 1380 Barstow Rd. in Barstow for $2.95 million. A local public college acquired the building which was formerly occupied by Rite-Aid. The retail building is located at the intersection of two major freeways, Interstate 15 and Interstate 40, which are traveled by approximately 19 million vehicles annually.  Additionally, over 60 million people stop, shop and dine in Barstow each year.  SVP Paul Galmarini of Progressive Real Estate represented the seller. The buyer was represented by George Okita and Sophia Heimall of California Commercial Real Estate Services. “Our comprehensive, out-of-the-box marketing program along with the college’s vision was instrumental in securing this deal,” said Galmarini. “The college was attracted to the property’s proximity to its main campus, boosting organic facilities’ growth for the college.” The post Local College Snaps Up Former Rite Aid in Barstow appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Local college purchases former Rite Aid in Barstow, CA for $2.95M (17,272 sq ft)
Site at I-15/I-40 intersection; 19M vehicles annually; 60M annual visitation

stories.summary: A Southern California public college acquired a 17,272-square-foot former Rite Aid building at 1380 Barstow Rd. for $2.95 million. The freestanding retail property sits at the intersection of Interstates 15 and 40, served by ~19 million vehicles annually. The college buyer was motivated by proximity to its main campus and plans for organic facilities growth.
stories.impact: Limited relevance to multifamily development. Institutional buyer (college) removing retail real estate from market reduces supply and may signal retail headwinds in secondary markets. No direct demand signal for apartments, but Barstow's position as a regional logistics/tourism hub (I-15/I-40 interchange) could support future workforce housing development if light industrial or distribution-center employment expands.

stories.title: Piedmont Buys Virginia Office for $53M — Double Its 2024 Sale Price
stories.excerpt: A joint venture has unloaded an office building in Northern Virginia for nearly twice what it paid to acquire the property just two years ago in the depths of post-pandemic distress. The venture involving FarmView Ventures, GreenBarn Investment Group and Rithm Capital sold the 189,000-square-foot, Class A office at 4075 Wilson Boulevard in Arlington, Va., for $52.7 million. The JV acquired the asset for $27.6 million in September 2024, property records show, and then completed about $6 million in renovations, as well as filled the retail space and closed 10 office leases. The building is approximately 83 percent leased and has 5.5 years of weighted-average lease term. The occupancy rate was reportedly 52 percent at the time of the 2024 sale. “This represents the first ‘round trip’ institutional sale of an office building in the region post-COVID market reset,” FarmView Ventures CEO John Wolf said in a social media post. Piedmont Realty Trust acquired the Wilson Boulevard asset in Arlington’s Ballston submarket, according to a Securities & Exchange Commission (SEC) filing. Tenants include defense contractor Systems Planning & Analysis, cybersecurity firm KnowBe4 and software company Nalej, while energy firm Argan moved its headquarters to the building last year. Ground-floor retail tenants include Sweetgreen, Van Leeuwen Ice Cream, Grazie Nonna and Pinnacle Bank. “The Ballston submarket continues to serve as a hub for defense and cybersecurity tenants,” the SEC filing read. “4075 Wilson is two blocks from the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency and Office of Naval Research.” Piedmont has a growing Ballston portfolio, including nearby office properties 3100 Clarendon Boulevard, 4250 North Fairfax Drive, and Arlington Gateway at 901 North Glebe Road. After ~$6 million in renovations and aggressive leasing (closing 10 office deals), the building reached 83% occupancy with a 5.5-year weighted-average lease term, up from 52% occupancy at acquisition.
stories.impact: Northern Virginia office turnaround signals selective institutional capital moving into stabilized, well-located Class A assets with short lease maturities—cap rates likely 4.5–5.5% range. For multifamily: office leasing strength in Ballston suggests employer demand and white-collar workforce retention; supports residential demand in Clarendon, Pentagon City, and nearby submarkets. However, institutional office buyer (Piedmont) targeting trophy assets; secondary office buildings remain untraded, signaling bifurcation—watch for office-to-residential conversion opportunities in weaker Ballston/Crystal City submarkets if office delivery overshoots.

stories.title: Harrison Street, U. of San Diego to Partner for On-Campus Housing
stories.excerpt: Harrison Street Asset Management and The Michaels Organization have formed a public-private partnership agreement with the University of San Diego to build the Presidio Terrace Apartments, a planned new $230 million, 321-unit, 700-bed on-campus student housing development. The investment represents the first transaction completed through Harrison Street’s dedicated public-private partnership strategy, as well as USD’s first-ever PPP agreement. Located on USD’s campus between the University’s academic center and a nearby retail corridor, Presidio Terrace will be the University’s latest on-campus residential facility purpose-built for upperclassmen, graduate and professional students. The development is expected to be completed in August 2029. “Presidio Terrace is a strong example of how PPPs can help universities address critical infrastructure needs, creating a win-win situation for academic institutions, investors, and college communities,” said Jim Hennessy, head of PPP business development at Harrison Street. “Today, we are seeing more PPP activity than ever before, as more universities recognize that these structures allow them to focus on their core academic mission while conserving capital and transferring operational responsibilities to a private partner.” The project is structured through a 99-year ground lease with USD and will benefit from a full real estate tax exemption as a University-affiliated facility. The property will be developed and operated by Michaels, with which Harrison Street has an extensive prior relationship and track record. Harrison Street, which is one of the largest owners of on-campus housing nationally, has been a long-term leader in the public-private partnership space, working with universities and other mission-driven institutions to develop and finance critical infrastructure while allowing those organizations to preserve capital for their core missions. stories.impact: University PPP model signals institutional capital targeting long-term, credit-backed multifamily cash flows (student housing) with reduced execution risk via established operators. San Diego market benefits from direct student-housing supply that offsets off-campus rental demand; however, PPP model diverts capital from traditional multifamily. Watch for operator/investor interest in USD-adjacent neighborhoods (Linda Vista, Fashion Valley submarkets) to capture spillover demand if on-campus housing underperforms or rates spike.

stories.title: Logos Faith Development CEO Martin Porter On Building With Religious Institutions
stories.excerpt: Faith-based development is having a moment in Southern California, where churches and other religious institutions control underused land in some of the communities most desperate for more housing. Logos Faith Development is partnering with these institutions rather than buying sites outright, and using those properties to develop mixed-income and affordable housing while returning value to the congregations and communities that own the land. Logos’ founder and CEO, Pastor Martin Porter, established the firm’s unusually selective model by way of commercial brokerage. After joining a South Los Angeles church, Porter said he saw persistent gaps facing faith-based organizations that wanted to develop their real estate but lacked the expertise. What began as a calling has grown into a for-profit development company with a roughly $750 million pipeline, 15 signed joint ventures expected to break ground through 2028, and dozens more church-owned sites under review. Commercial Observer spoke with Porter in August about why faith-owned land can be the key to unlocking difficult affordable housing deals, and how Logos structures returns for both investors and churches. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. Commercial Observer: You came to Logos after working in commercial brokerage and entering African Methodist Episcopal ministry. How did those paths come together? Martin C. Porter: At a time in my life when I really committed myself to service and to serving a higher power and trying to do more than just transactions, I joined a church in South L.A. and entered into ministry. As part of that process, I saw there was really a knowledge, commitment and financial gap in faith-based development, and I was invited in by churches to help them solve the problem. So it was sort of kismet. bullets: Logos Faith Development: ~$750M pipeline, 15 signed JVs with churches through 2028
Founder Pastor Martin Porter partners with faith institutions vs. buying land outright
Model targets mixed-income/affordable housing on underused religious-institution sites in SoCal
stories.summary: Logos Faith Development, founded by Pastor Martin Porter, has built a roughly $750 million pipeline by partnering with churches and religious institutions on their underused land rather than acquiring sites directly. The company has 15 signed joint ventures expected to break ground through 2028 and dozens more church-owned sites under review. The model focuses on mixed-income and affordable housing while returning value to congregations and communities.
stories.impact: Faith-institution partnership model unlocks land supply in supply-constrained Southern California neighborhoods—churches control underused urban and suburban sites with soft ownership dynamics (mission-aligned, patient capital, tax incentives). This reduces per-unit land cost and entitlement friction, enabling affordable/mixed-income development viability in markets where market-rate development alone is constrained. For institutional developers: faith JV model competes directly with traditional land acquisition; monitor pipeline acceleration and yield (IRR vs. cap rate) to gauge capital reallocation risk. Affordable housing supply in SoCal improves, potentially moderating total renter-income requirements and compressing market-rate rents in adjacent submarkets.

stories.title: Kirkland & Ellis Hires Seth Niedermayer as Partner in Real Estate Group
stories.excerpt: After more than a decade at HSF Kramer, real estate attorney Seth Niedermayer has moved offices to Kirkland & Ellis. Niedermayer joined the Chicago-based law firm’s real estate group as a partner this week, as shared in a LinkedIn post Monday evening and confirmed by a spokesperson for the firm. Kirkland & Ellis, which serves a range of clients in private equity and corporate transactions, is based at 601 Lexington Avenue and will operate a growing second New York City practice at 900 Third Avenue once that office opens. At Kirkland & Ellis, Niedermayer will represent private equity and investor clients, as well as developers and operators, across real estate transactions, according to a spokesperson for the firm. His primary focus will be joint ventures and financing. “Kirkland has an unrivaled platform to serve clients on their most sophisticated and important matters, and I’m excited to collaborate with the firm’s exceptionally talented lawyers,” Niedermayer told Commercial Observer in a statement. “I look forward to bringing my experience to the team and continuing to build on the firm’s tremendous momentum in real estate.” Niedermayer’s move follows more than a decade of work at HSF Kramer, which was still Kramer Levin Naftalis & Frankel when he arrived as an associate in 2015. He had limited real estate experience then, Niedermayer told CO in June, but the firm’s practice evolved alongside the real estate market — particularly as private capital gained dominance. He was made partner in 2022. During his tenure, Niedermayer represented Mitsui Fudosan America in its joint venture at 50 Hudson Yards. He also worked on Vici Properties and Apollo Global Management’s acquisition of the Venetian on the Las Vegas Strip in 2022. “For more than a decade, Seth has been a valued member of our real estate practice, and we’re grateful for his contributions to the firm and our clients,” Jay Neveloff, chair of U.S. real estate at HSF Kramer, told CO
bullets: Seth Niedermayer joins Kirkland & Ellis as real estate partner from HSF Kramer (11+ yrs)
Focus: PE/investor clients, developers, operators; joint ventures and financing transactions

stories.summary: Seth Niedermayer, a real estate attorney with over 11 years at HSF Kramer, joined Kirkland & Ellis as a partner in the firm's real estate group. He will represent private equity, investors, developers, and operators across real estate transactions, with primary focus on joint ventures and financing. Kirkland & Ellis is expanding its New York City practice.
stories.impact: Limited relevance to multifamily development. Law firm lateral hires indicate market activity (JV and financing volume) but do not signal rent, supply, or capital-cost shifts. However, KE's expanded NYC practice and focus on PE/JV and financing transactions suggest capital is flowing into real estate; multifamily financing and partnership activity in Northeast likely remains robust, supporting debt and equity availability.

stories.title: Podcast: How AI Is Making Rental Application Fraud Harder to Catch, with Docuverus
stories.excerpt: Jamie Borodin is the founder and CEO of Docuverus, a document verification and fraud detection platform purpose-built for multifamily housing providers. With over 30 years in resident screening, Jamie founded Docuverus in 2017 to address a gap no existing tool was solving: authenticating income documents at the metadata level while simultaneously reading and calculating their contents. Docuverus is one of the only platforms with a direct connection to the Social Security Administration for synthetic identity detection. Jamie is based in southern New Jersey. bullets: Docuverus CEO Jamie Borodin: AI-generated income fraud harder to detect; synthetic identities rising
Fraud hotspots: Houston, Atlanta; NYC different; 30+ years resident screening experience

stories.summary: Docuverus CEO Jamie Borodin discussed how AI-generated documents and synthetic identities are making rental application fraud harder to detect. The platform authenticates income documents at the metadata level while simultaneously reading and calculating their contents, and maintains a direct connection to the Social Security Administration for synthetic identity detection. Fraud hotspots include Houston and Atlanta; NYC patterns differ.
stories.impact: Rising synthetic-identity and AI-generated income fraud signals operational risk for multifamily operators—underwriting reserves and bad-debt losses may increase if screening tools lag fraud sophistication. Houston and Atlanta multifamily operators face elevated tenant-qualification risk; tightening screening standards (higher credit scores, income multiples, guarantors) may reduce applicant pool and lengthen leasing cycles. Operators should invest in metadata and SSA-verification tooling to mitigate credit losses and maintain pricing power—expect screening-technology costs to rise as a % of CAC.
